reference.source: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology / WHO laboratory manual for semen analysis
clinicalPearls: Organic erectile dysfunction typically develops gradually, is present in most sexual situations, and is accompanied by loss of spontaneous nocturnal and early-morning erections
By contrast, a psychogenic pattern is often abrupt, situational, and retains nocturnal erections, though many men have a mixed picture
The commonest organic mechanism is vascular, and dysfunction frequently precedes overt coronary or peripheral arterial disease, serving as an early marker of endothelial disease
Every man presenting with erectile dysfunction should undergo cardiovascular risk assessment, as the small penile arteries may signal disease in larger vessels before symptoms elsewhere
Diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, smoking, obesity, and hypogonadism are important and often modifiable contributors
A directed history, examination, and measurement of morning testosterone and metabolic parameters identify most causes without invasive testing

First-line treatment is with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors alongside risk-factor modification, with intracavernosal or intraurethral agents, vacuum devices, and penile prosthesis reserved for non-responders
Coexisting hypogonadism should be corrected as it can both cause dysfunction and reduce the response to oral therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Penile erection is a neurovascular event in which parasympathetic and nitric-oxide-mediated signalling relaxes cavernosal smooth muscle, allowing arterial inflow to engorge the sinusoids and compress the subtunical venules to trap blood. Organic erectile dysfunction arises when any component of this pathway is impaired. Vasculogenic disease, driven by atherosclerosis and endothelial dysfunction, reduces arterial inflow and impairs the veno-occlusive mechanism. Neurogenic causes interrupt the autonomic and somatic innervation, as after pelvic surgery, in diabetes, or with neurological disease. Endocrine causes, chiefly testosterone deficiency and hyperprolactinaemia, blunt libido and the erectile response. Because the cavernosal arteries are of small calibre, endothelial compromise manifests here early, which is why organic erectile dysfunction commonly heralds systemic cardiovascular disease.
additionalDifferentials: Peyronie disease and other penile structural disorders
Medication-induced dysfunction, including antihypertensives and antidepressants
Chronic systemic disease such as renal or hepatic failure
Neurological disease or the aftermath of pelvic surgery
Substance-related causes including alcohol and recreational drugs
additionalInvestigations: Focused history including onset, situational variation, and nocturnal erections, with a validated symptom questionnaire
Early-morning serum testosterone, repeated if low, with luteinising hormone and prolactin where indicated
Fasting glucose or HbA1c and a lipid profile to assess cardiometabolic risk
Blood pressure measurement and cardiovascular risk stratification
Penile duplex Doppler ultrasound in selected men where a primary vascular cause needs confirmation
Review of current medications for erectile side effects
Thyroid and renal function where systemic disease is suspected
redFlags: Erectile dysfunction as a sentinel symptom of undiagnosed cardiovascular disease requiring cardiac assessment
Associated symptoms of hypogonadism or a pituitary lesion such as visual disturbance
New neurological signs pointing to spinal or central disease
Penile deformity, pain, or plaque suggesting Peyronie disease
Priapism or a history of prolonged erections as a treatment complication
reference.prognosis: Most men respond well to phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and risk-factor modification, and identifying and treating the underlying cardiometabolic disease benefits overall health; where oral therapy fails, injectable agents, devices, and prosthetic surgery offer highly effective alternatives.
pitfalls: Treating erectile dysfunction symptomatically without assessing cardiovascular risk
Overlooking coexisting hypogonadism that reduces the response to oral therapy
Missing a culprit medication that could be changed
Attributing an organic problem to psychological causes and delaying appropriate investigation
Failing to counsel on priapism and nitrate interactions before prescribing phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors
references: European Association of Urology guidelines on sexual and reproductive health
International guidance on erectile dysfunction and cardiovascular risk
